title.value: Social isolation and the brain in the pandemic era
title.justification: The title was explicitly mentioned at the beginning of the paper and throughout the document.
title.quote: Social isolation and the brain in the pandemic era

analysis.description: This review article outlines the impact of social isolation on the human brain during the COVID-19 pandemic, emphasizing the neurobiological and psychological consequences of prolonged social deprivation. It focuses on evolutionary perspectives of human sociality, the neural basis of social isolation, and the broader social implications related to public health measures.

type.justification: The paper reviews existing research on social isolation, its evolutionary basis, and neurobiological mechanisms without conducting new empirical investigations.
type.quote: We then review defining features of that human sociality, putting forward a framework within which one can understand the consequences of mass social isolation during the COVID-19 pandemic.

name.justification: The paper extensively discusses the neural basis of social behavior and the impacts of isolation on brain structures and functions.
name.quote: We outline recent research on the neural basis of prolonged social isolation...highlighting especially higher-order neural circuits such as the default mode network.

name.justification: The paper discusses psychological outcomes related to social isolation, such as loneliness and mental health impacts.
name.quote: Including mental health deterioration, stress, sleep disturbance and substance misuse.

name.justification: The paper discusses social structures and networks, and their importance for human health and well-being.
name.quote: The structure of our social world...provides an important framework that helps explain some of the consequences of social isolation.

name.justification: The UK Biobank is mentioned in the analysis of brain and psychological data related to social isolation impacts.
name.quote: A Bayesian hierarchical model was applied to ~40,000 UK Biobank participants to distinguish lonely (target group, encoded as 1) from non-lonely participants (control group, encoded as 0).
